consensus_summary: All four blind responses agree that Gehenna is the Valley of Hinnom—notorious for child sacrifice to Molech/Baal and renamed the Valley of Slaughter in Jeremiah's oracles—which became the standard New Testament symbol for final, post-judgment divine punishment of the wicked ('hell'), depicted with unquenchable fire, the undying worm, and destruction of body and soul. They note internal debates (eternal torment vs. annihilation vs. remedial fire vs. AD 70 historical judgment) and that Gehenna is distinguished from Hades/Sheol as the intermediate state of the dead.
book_summary: The book identifies Gehenna as 'a valley-trial carried through to a destructive verdict': the literal Valley of Hinnom at Jerusalem's boundary, site of counterfeit worship and child sacrifice, renamed Valley of Slaughter, which pictures the judgment that destroys both body and soul. It explicitly distinguishes Gehenna from Sheol, which holds the dead.
consensus_core_identification: Gehenna = the Valley of Hinnom (child sacrifice; Jeremiah's Valley of Slaughter) functioning as the symbol of God's final punitive judgment on the wicked after death, distinct from Sheol/Hades.
book_core_identification: Gehenna = the Valley of Hinnom (counterfeit-worship child sacrifice; renamed Valley of Slaughter) picturing the judgment that destroys both body and soul, distinct from Sheol which holds the dead.
boundary_disagreement: None of substance. The book's phrase 'destroys both soul and body' (echoing Matthew 10:28) could be read as leaning toward a destruction/annihilation emphasis rather than eternal conscious torment, but this remains within the consensus's own primary basis texts and does not alter which referent or which cases Gehenna covers. The book also declines to specify duration or mechanism, which the consensus itself flags as the unsettled sub-question.
material_contradiction: None. Both identify the same historical valley with the same OT associations as the symbol of final destructive judgment, and both distinguish it from Sheol/Hades.
rationale: Reduced to their minimum cores, both readings say the same thing: the Valley of Hinnom, defiled by child sacrifice and prophetically renamed the Valley of Slaughter, symbolizes God's final judgment on the wicked—the New Testament 'hell.' The book's distinctive framing ('valley-trial carried through to a destructive verdict') is stylistic, and its explicit Sheol distinction mirrors Response A's note distinguishing Gehenna from Sheol/Hades. The book does not adopt the discredited garbage-dump etiology, adds no new referent, and excludes no cases the consensus admits. The 'destroys both body and soul' language quotes Matthew 10:28 directly rather than staking a contested annihilationist claim; even if read that way, it would fall within a listed alternative and the consensus's cited texts, not a boundary change to the core identification.
strongest_objection: One could argue the book's choice to define the judgment as one that 'destroys both body and soul,' with no mention of eternal conscious punishment, quietly narrows the consensus's dominant eternal-torment reading toward an annihilationist boundary, which would make the entry REFINED rather than MATCH. But since the entry merely paraphrases Matthew 10:28—a verse every consensus response lists as primary basis—and takes no explicit position on duration, this objection over-reads the compressed glossary wording.
